headline: High-risk shared write/network surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and agent_a also uses MCP plus browser/web surfaces, so content from one can plausibly be consumed by the other as instructions. Agent_b lacks MCP and browser, which lowers direct bridging, but shared filesystem/workspace pathways remain enough for injection risk in default use.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory, injection risk is present.
IF agent_b ingests file contents from agent_a without provenance checks, malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic execution of file-sourced instructions.
Add provenance labels to shared artifacts.
Review any MCP-fed content before use.
requires-engineering: enforce sandboxed, read-only handoff channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a handles API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and workspace files; agent_b handles configuration secrets and academic content. Because both can read/write files and agent_a has broad network egress, a shared workspace or copied artifacts can leak sensitive data across the pair in default setups.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem or mounted workspace, sensitive files can cross between them.
IF agent_a exports copied context over the network, secrets may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate secret stores per agent.
Mount only the minimum required directories.
Redact secrets before any handoff.
Turn off broad egress where possible.
requires-engineering: add DLP and per-agent access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, so concurrent edits to shared files are plausible. Agent_a can also modify git state while agent_b cannot, which reduces symmetry but not conflict if they share a repo or workspace. No locking is stated, so write collisions are a realistic default risk.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF agent_a commits while agent_b edits the same tree, git state conflicts can arise.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Serialize write phases manually.
Avoid concurrent git operations.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_b is a content-writing/RAG workflow that can plausibly consume outputs from agent_a, and agent_a can generate web- or file-derived content that may be treated as authoritative. The pair lacks any documented verification boundary, so errors can cascade from agent_a into agent_b outputs or actions.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a-produced text as source material, errors can be amplified.
IF agent_a's outputs are published or acted on without verification, downstream mistakes persist.
mitigations: Require human review of cross-agent outputs.
Add citation checks before publication.
Keep source provenance with each artifact.
Use a verification step between agents.
requires-engineering: implement automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a touches audit logs, conversation history, and secrets in a sales-CRM context, while agent_b handles academic papers, metadata, and configuration secrets in a local development environment. The profiles show different data classes and likely retention/logging expectations, but no direct residency or certification mismatch is documented, so the safest supported rating is medium.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is routed through both agents, retention or logging mismatches can occur.
IF either agent stores data longer than the other expects, compliance drift is present.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it.
Align retention settings across both agents.
Disable unnecessary logging.
Keep regulated data out of the content-writing workflow.
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA boundaries.
